title: Validation, Sanitization, and Encoding (Different Purposes)
learningObjectives: Explain the core ideas and terminology of validation, sanitization, and encoding (different purposes).
Recognize the risks or mistakes this topic is intended to prevent.
Apply appropriate defensive practices in a beginner project.
Distinguish this topic from related security concepts and controls.
Review a simple design and justify improvements using evidence.

understand.concept: Validation checks whether input meets rules; sanitization transforms input to remove or normalize unwanted parts when that transformation is appropriate; encoding represents data safely for a specific output context. These are not interchangeable. Prefer allowlists and explicit type/range checks. Output encoding must match the destination context, such as HTML text, attributes, URLs, or SQL parameters. Avoid trying to make all input 'safe' with one universal transformation.
understand.whyItMatters: Using the wrong technique can leave vulnerabilities or corrupt legitimate data.
understand.analogy: Think of a careful community space where entry, use of shared items, and privacy are guided by clear rules and appropriate checks.
understand.analogyLimit: Software security depends on technical boundaries, data flows, implementation details, and changing threats that this analogy cannot fully represent.

explain.narrative:
Validation checks whether input meets rules; sanitization transforms input to remove or normalize unwanted parts when that transformation is appropriate; encoding represents data safely for a specific output context. These are not interchangeable. Prefer allowlists and explicit type/range checks. Output encoding must match the destination context, such as HTML text, attributes, URLs, or SQL parameters. Avoid trying to make all input 'safe' with one universal transformation.

Apply these principles proportionately. Use established platform and library protections instead of improvising security-critical mechanisms. For a real application, confirm requirements and review the implementation with qualified peers.

commonMistakes: Assuming a feature is safe because it works in normal use.
Trusting client-side controls as the only enforcement.
Applying one generic transformation to every kind of input or output.
Exposing credentials or personal data in source, logs, or screenshots.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Create validation rules for a display name, age, and category. Decide which transformations are normalization, validation, and output encoding. Explain why a single function cannot safely do all three.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Design input handling for a comment form. Write an allowlist/range/length policy and describe output encoding for HTML text. Use trusted library/platform helpers in real applications.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy project and no real secrets or personal data.
Design input handling for a comment form. Write an allowlist/range/length policy and describe output encoding for HTML text. Use trusted library/platform helpers in real applications.

questions.prompt: Why is sanitization not a universal security solution?
options: Different contexts require different controls and transformations
It always removes too much
It cannot change strings
It is the same as authorization
questions.answer: Different contexts require different controls and transformations
questions.explanation: There is no one transformation that safely handles all destinations.

options: A set of explicitly permitted categories
Any string that is not empty
All input except a known bad phrase
A random value
questions.answer: A set of explicitly permitted categories

questions.prompt: What is a safe database input practice?
options: Use parameterized queries supported by the database API
Build SQL by concatenating user text
Remove every space
Hide the query in the UI
questions.answer: Use parameterized queries supported by the database API
questions.explanation: Parameterization keeps values separate from query structure.
